Achieving precise cosmological inferences using Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) requires accounting for gravitational lensing, a factor that feeble lensing amplification has long been recognized to influence. Although too faint to observe individually, the collective signal of this lensing was recently demonstrated using the Pantheon sample, which tracked 1049 SNe Ia across 1049 unique hosts (some appearing multiple times). This study re-examines those 1049 events by utilizing recent, comprehensive estimates of the matter distribution from over 3 million galaxy cluster members. Adoptating a rigorous statistical approach that properly handles the non-Gaussian and asymmetric error distribution of these lensing estimates, we derived point-estimates for the cosmic stochastic lensing signal, yielding parameters for mean magnification ($\langle A \rangle$) and its scatter ($\sigma_A$). The analysis refines the recent measurement by Escamilla et al. (2021b), yielding $\sigma_A \approx 0.17 \pm 0.01$, a value consistent with independent theoretical predictions. These novel, robust statistics provide an essential foundation for upcoming, larger surveys of type Ia supernovae.

We studied the effect of moral principles on ideal rejection rates in kidney pairing, formulating an integrated framework of kidney pairing and four distinct deontological theories to evaluate policy efficacy. In a multi-player extensive-form game, an agent rationalizably selects an action that best responds to the strategies of others, considering only those that themselves respond reasonably to further levels. Within such extensive games, a strategy profile where every participant has a unique best response to the remaining rational options is known as a single-equilibrium strategy profile (SES). While SES represents a stable solution within these dynamic interactions, existing algorithms take an exponentially long time—specifically exponential relative to the extensive game's extensive nature—even if the number of players remains small and the action counts per player are low. To rectify this inefficiency, we present a3 algorithm that runs in time polynomial with respect to both the number of players and their respective action counts, albeit extensive with the total number of actions. Specifically, this new approach introduces "evidence concepts," a new concept equivalent to rationalizable equilibria but more efficient for computation. By basing calculations on matrix data structures containing only the payoffs of pertinent actions, the efficiency of our algorithm improves to the 5 complexity, which is non-dependent on the extensive nature of game play. Consequently, this method enables multiple players to be engaged in extensive games while efficiently identifying a unique best strategy profile (SES).

WorkingWiki serves as an open, collaborative research environment built specifically upon the MediaWiki engine and a suite of proprietary enhancements, often functioning as a essential companion to academic publications. Initially established in 2016 to support an IEEE Transactions article, it maintained active public use for over four years, accumulating more than a thousand pages and ten thousand contributions from approximately eight hundred unique authors. While heavily relying on standard MediaWiki capabilities, the platform also integrates several custom components, most significantly "ResearchCite," a dynamic referencing tool that automatically manages, formats, and resolves connections between writings and bibfiles within the wiki ecosystem. Further custom developments addressed functional gaps, enhancing capabilities for structured data input, advanced search mechanisms, rights management, customizable interface modules, and real-time communication channels such as chat, video conferencing, and task tracking. Distinctly different from the traditional "read-only" model of conventional Wikis, WorkingWiki is engineered for constant co-authorship and collaboration among experts in a "write-centric" research paradigm, facilitating what we term a "wiki-based collective authoring" (WCA) process. Through this model, contributors engage in iterative feedback loops, refining a draft "working paper" through sustained dialogue, formal reviews, and consensus building until reaching a stage suitable for submission to academic venues. We present a comprehensive overview of the WorkingWiki infrastructure, detailing its technical architecture, operational dynamics, and the characteristics of its extensive, diverse contributor base.

We propose a co-associative analysis strategy that integrates functional genomics with genome-wide association studies (GWAS). The KSI (Knowability-Scarcity-Importance) metric was defined to rank single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), factoring known functional data, GWAS evidence, and additional sources to estimate the retrievability and abundance of such data. In this work, we compare the resulting SNP rankings for eight neuroticism, heart rate variation (HRV), and blood pressure (BP)-related GWAS against restative scenarios including eight anthropometric measurements such as height. Results indicate that SNP importance assessments significantly improve when grounded in underlying biological functions, a effect particularly pronounced for the associations regarding neuroticism, HRV, and BP; this demonstrates the position-sensitive nature of our metric and highlights how reliance on importance estimates varies with the prevalence and data-pastigance of SNPs. Finally, we highlight eight traits—QR, BP, height, weight, fat mass (FM), FM percentage, areal bone mineral density (aBMD), and areal areal bone mineral density (aBMD)) as a set of related genomic markers that may share regulatory networks, with implications for understanding their shared heritability.

The Large Hadron Collider's (LHC) ability to explore small systems has been a key aspect since inception, involving the examination of proton-proton (pp) collisions at extreme centralities, proton ions (pA) interactions, and heavy ion ions (AA) collisions at reduced energies. These efforts aim to ascertain if the unique properties of quark-gluon plasma (QGP)—a state characterized by lack of particle type dependence—the existence of gluon saturation effects, and the presence of particle production mechanisms exist in these minor systems. This review examines the distinctive features, phenomena, and theoretical frameworks relevant to these small systems, comparing them alongside more extensive proton protons and proton ion systems.

We conduct an analysis of quiescent X-ray location at Galactic masses using data provided by Pal et al. (2018). By cross-referencing this dataset with literature findings on associated transient events, we establish a clear correlation in the relationship $P_{orb} \sim E_{\dot{g}}$ near the 45-degree divide. This correlation distinctly separates systems with mass accretion from those without, implying a dichotomy defined at exactly the same boundary. Focusing exclusively on these quiescent systems at high mass allows us to refine existing constraints regarding the 30-day cycle observed in Blandford and Reipols (1994), assuming these systems possess high inclination and short timescales. Such systems are characterized as high mass ratio objects with mass < 1.4 $M_\odot$, extending to lower limits of the relationship $P_{orb} \sim E_{\dot{g}}$. These systems form a major component of the population described earlier, implying that the majority of such systems lack mass accretion mechanisms despite being present near the 45-degree divide. Such systems could include the most common type of object, yet they remain unexplained by the relation $P_{orb} \sim E_{\dot{g}}$.

We introduce methods enhancing the resolution and sensitivity of infrared and terahertz spectra to overcome these limitations. Applying this refined approach to silicon, I demonstrate the direct measurement of electron-phonon inertia, revealing correlations that would remain hidden using conventional techniques.

Researching semantic diversity presents a hurdle: without annotated paraphrases, existing approaches relying on supervised natural language inference for variety are constrained. To overcome this, we apply natural language inference to textual representations—such as graph embeddings and semantic encodings—extracted from graph-based methods. We posit that integrating graph-based vertex embedding conversational embeddings with natural language inference can effectively assess variety. The benchmark consists of open, turn-based dialogue tasks where we analyze the impact of different representation methods and inference algorithms on scoring a model's generation diversity. Our work presents extensive comparisons and offer comprehensive guidelines for utilizing the SeMico benchmark in future studies.

Bipedal locomotion represents an effective and versatile form of mobile operation, although it faces significant challenges due to low fuel efficiency and a lack of reliability. This paper introduces a novel concept utilizing propellant assistance to overcomes those issues. Initially, we establish the theoretical framework for achieving stable, propulsion-assisted walking. We demonstrate that injecting linear impulses during the stance phase can simultaneously reduce both the step's flight duration and its support phase duration. A specific condition is derived to guarantee stability after such impulsive modifications. Furthermore, we define a theoretical upper limit on the maximum jump capacity required to execute this form of locomotion efficiently. In practical application models, results indicate that optimizing trajectory planning to minimize total fuel consumption leads to shorter contact times on the ground. Ultimately, our approach offers a promising strategy to realize locomotion that is both highly efficient and robust.

This study introduces HyperDegrade, a software framework that transforms high-performance central processing unit (CPU) operating rates into significantly lower, yet still functional, frequencies. By systematically deactivating specific instructions within a CPU branch misprediction penalty handler, HyperDegrade reduces the cost associated with mispredictions. The resulting decrease in raw clock speed—from gigahertz ranges down to megahertz—has negligible impacts on well-behaved, pipeline-friendly code sequences but can effectively accelerate programs characterized by frequent branch mispredictions that would otherwise suffer performance degradation at reduced frequencies. HyperDegrade operates as a kernel module and delivers substantial speedups, sometimes exceeding a factor of three, for workloads experiencing high rates of branch mispredictions at lower frequencies.

A central challenge in multi-agent robotics is enabling heterogeneous teams to tackle tasks that demand joint computation and communication. This issue becomes even more complex as agent-to-agent data exchange consumes valuable resources. To navigate these complexities and enhance overall system performance through inter-agent cooperation, this paper introduces a family of algorithms. Our approach incorporates methods to establish optimal, efficient agent pairings, drawing on the concept of a tactical layer situated between upper strategy and lower execution levels of the architecture. This intermediate layer bridges the gap: while the top level defines general objectives, the bottom level handles concrete actions, allowing our proposed scheme to align overarching goals with executable steps. Furthermore, as this method operates as an overlay on any existing bottom-level architecture, it offers significant flexibility. We evaluate the scheme within a group of vacuum cleaning agents. Our evaluation metrics compare communication volume, execution efficiency, and collaboration quality against a popular commercial solution, demonstrating both computational superiority and higher cleaning efficiency in specific scenarios. These findings confirm the validity of the proposed algorithm using a standard household robot platform.

Vertical Federated Learning (FEDL) has attracted significant interest due to its ability to foster collaboration among parties who hold disjoint user databases, thereby fostering joint modeling while safeguarding individual data silos. Nevertheless, these participants remain susceptible to privacy breaches where an adversary extracts information regarding non-existent users, potentially utilizing such insights for targeted attacks. Drawing a parallel to previous work in horizontal federated settings, we investigate similar intrusive activities but distinguish ourselves by accounting for the unique structural constraints inherent to vertical scenarios. Specifically, we analyze the implications under the assumption that an attacker possesses additional data on a subset of target individuals—an attribute that sets vertical federated learning apart from horizontal counterparts. These approaches yielded a performance increase from the baseline 26.5 to 34.6%, successfully meeting our target of machine common if-then knowledge.

The Heston model serves as a foundational framework for evaluating risk, a focus that has dominated academic research for years. To validate our approach, we compare it against standard "brute force" techniques. This study focuses on establishing an operational two-qubit encoding for a truncated superconducting phase qubit. We further demonstrated the ability to execute two-qubit quantum gates utilizing this subspace, bounded by a short gate time of 100 $\mu$s and an estimated total error rate below 1%. The concept of metric dimension was originally introduced by Harary and Rodemich in 1975 along with their related findings, defining it as the smallest possible cardinality for a resolving set within a graph. A subset $S$ functions as resolving set for graph $G$ if, for any pair of distinct vertices $u$ and $w$ inside $G$, there exists some vertex $v$ within $S$ such that distance $d(v, u)$ does not equal distance $d(v, w)$. The metric dimension represents the minimum cardinality applicable to these resolving sets. This paper examines the metric dimension in relation to specific graph characteristics and structures, simultaneously investigating the metric dimension associated with graphs constructed through specified operations.

We address the difficulty of generalizing across environments by introducing an extension to the Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) 5th Edition core rules that formalizes intents and theory-of-mind (ToM). Knotted proteins are a functional class where understanding how knot formation occurs and how knotted regions interact with the rest of the chain is crucial. Since bending follows specific geometric and topological rules, we hypothesize that natural unknotted states of foldable proteins will produce knot-like curves upon folding, while kinkable states will produce swirl-like curves. Furthermore, because knotted proteins require bending rather than sharp kinks to form their structures, we propose using this distinction—between bendability and knokability—as a predictive guide for expected structural curves. Support for these proposals was provided through calculations demonstrating that the precursors of protein knots exhibit high values for the absolute average total link crossing when in their minimal energy condition. We also observed similar patterns where protein dislocations exhibit high linking values for the potential paths of travel. Additionally, we found consistent correlations between the depth of protein folds and the magnitude of bending versus twisting parameters. These results suggest we should examine other biologically important linear polymers, such as DNA, to investigate if similar geometric correlations help explain structural formation processes.

We validated our approach in real-world scenarios through extensive experiments, demonstrating its superiority over current mobile HDR fusion techniques.

We introduce L2Explorer, a benchmark framework designed to assess whether a reinforcement learning (RL) agent can adapt to new sub-environments within the same type of environment by learning from prior experience. We define an "sub-environment" through a shift in the optimal policy, causing performance on previously mastered tasks to decline unless effective transfer learning is applied. Our framework evaluates three distinct learning strategies: utilizing only the best-performing policy, employing standard online learning algorithms, and applying our specific transfer learning approach. Results from L2Explorer demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms both baseline approaches in maintaining stability and keeping optimal performance across environments of this category. Furthermore, we observe that agents utilizing online learning struggle with environments when the optimal policy shifts only slightly, whereas those using our method can acquire consistent and high-level performance even with minimal data samples in similar settings.

In today's information landscape, the rapid dissemination of news across social media platforms significantly impacts public sentiment and events; however, this acceleration also facilitates the spread of misinformation. Traditional news verification methods often require a cyclical process involving multiple versions, which is impractical for immediate alerting on newly published stories. In contrast, our study focuses on identifying whether a specific news item is authentic or false immediately upon release, utilizing concurrent multimodal inputs such as text and web-searched images/gens. We introduce two primary contributions: first, the False News Binary Task (FNBT), which frames misinformation detection as a binary classification challenge instead of a generative issue, and second, the Meta Neural Process (MNpT) model designed to harness cross-modal feature representations to supply missing information. This approach, demonstrated through experiments on two standard benchmarks, yields superior outcomes regarding news fact-checking, supporting the hypothesis that emergent knowledge can be fostered through multimodal integration to detect misinformation.

Recently, various topological distinctness indicators indicating non-trivial behavior have been identified within the conjugacy classes of a periodic conveyance operator. We establish several upper bounds for the maximum cardinality of polyphase Golay complementary sets that form a mutually Golay complementary (MGC) set with given base size $d$. Specifically, these limits apply when expanding from an initial collection of $d$ Golay complementary sets of length $N$. By combining these limits with outcomes from other research, we determine precise limits for creating polyphase MGC sets of size size $d$ and code length $N$. Additionally, we prove the existence of structured sets with specific properties that help define creative constructions for such families.

Silicon's energy band structure includes elliptic k=0 valleys at the X-point in the Brillouin zone, which have attracted significant interest due to their promising properties for both fundamental research and scalable quantum computing. Recent advances now allow the isolated control of individual quantum valleys in silicon nanodevises, forming a "valley atom," although understanding how these vacancies interact at atomic levels remains incomplete. Using gate-defined silicon nanodot systems, we investigate spin-to-valley conversion between an electron confined in a localized orbital and non-occupied band valleys. Our analysis demonstrates that Coulomb repulsion between an occupied site and a neighbor, combined to orbital confinement forces, induces a coupling between a localized spin and free band valleys—mechanisms analogous to superexchange or tunneling-induced coupling. These observed spin-erval interaction effects are specific to silicon; they do not occur in wider band materials like GaAs. Furthermore, the interaction strengths we measure provide crucial data for validating *ab initio* band structure calculations.

The analytical and predictive capabilities graph neural networks (GNNs) offer for dynamic complex systems have established them as a vital research focus across academic and industrial sectors. However, a comprehensive framework connecting a system's inherent dynamics to its GNN-based modeling methods is still absent. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Concept Laser Scanner (CLS), a system analysis framework designed to identify and classify prominent dynamic patterns within systems. LLM's hold much promise in assisting humans, yet their utility is limited without integrated factual knowledge. Existing approaches fall short by failing to reflect the interconnected web of human knowledge. We present a structured framework to resolve this issue and introduce a flexible, modular architecture for data processes termed Ability. This system handles [i.] the creation of graph-based representations from unstructured natural language inputs through advanced parsing techniques [ii.] the development of structured, expert-like capabilities where specific graph sub-components function together to master a distinct ability, and [iii.] the systematic embedding of these capabilities into an base architecture like GPT-2. We validate our method's scalability in creating hundreds of new abilities and demonstrate that a small "Ability-GPT" model, trained solely on relatively minor incorporated knowledge, can significantly surpass both standard LLM baselines (50% F1) and the upper bounds (150% improvement in capability) of existing methods at solving tasks requiring integrated knowledge.

This research explores spatial anti-alasing techniques for rendering line junctions on vector maps, a component frequently overlooked yet visually critical in rendering map data. While previous work has addressed anti-alasing for lines, curves, and polygons independently, the unique visual characteristics and rendering requirements specific to line junctions remain unstudied. Line junctions represent a fundamental element in vector map data structures; therefore, mastering their smooth display is essential for high-quality navigation and location-based services. Our approach treats line junctions and line segments as a unified entity, calculating both their width and orientation relative to neighboring junction parts to address challenges caused by screen resolution variations, screen angles, and the discrepancies between vector coordinates and pixel values. This method effectively renders complex networks, including intersecting lines, T-junctions, and various terminal points, offering a cost-efficient anti-alasing solution that can be broadly applied in real-world systems.

We introduce Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN), an advanced model for single-aspect speech enhancement. Our approach addresses the known slow training speeds of End-to-End Deep Recurrent Networks (EDRN) and the limited performance of standard Convolutional Recurrent Networks (CRN) on complex acoustic interference. The design of DPCRN integrates both an End-to-End Deep Recurrent module, which captures subtle non-linear patterns, and a Convolutional Recurrent module, which efficiently handles significant non-Stationary noise characteristics. Evaluations in realistic environments demonstrate a 0.22 increase in Short-Time Objective Intelligibility (STOI) and 0.1 improvement in MOS scores for enhanced audio compared to existing baseline models, with results showing 9.5% faster training speed-up as well. DPCRN exhibits remarkable robustness across diverse and noisy conditions, making it an optimal solution for enhancing isolated voice streams.

Recent initiatives aim to extend Single-column Models (SCMs) of atmospheric convection to include multiple fluid levels, thereby accounting for surface-based processes like the thermal soil layer or mixed seab. The application of this simple two-fluid framework holds significant utility, potentially offering a practical tool for convection modeling in advanced Earth System Models.

Influence function methods offer a promising pathway to fine-tune pre-trained deep neural network models on tasks like classification and regression while requiring minimal computational power compared to gradient-based approaches that use actual data. However, these methods currently assume the labels of fine-tuning data are known a priori, a limitation that excludes many real-world scenarios where annotation costs are prohibitive or labels are inaccessible. This paper introduces a novel label-agnostic fine-tuning strategy that leverages data clustering to harness only the most valuable subsets of new inputs for adaptation. The proposed algorithm computes influence functions across a batch of fine-tuning samples to identify those highly impactful instances, iteratively refining both their selection and quantity through an self-similar clustering mechanism until a stopping criterion is met. Experimental results drawn from cat-dog and natural language processing benchmarks demonstrate that this label-free clustering framework attains a substantial speedup while preserving nearly the same precision as label-guided counterparts when processing fine-tuning batches of thirty samples. Furthermore, when applied to larger, unannotated datasets, the approach enables effective learning with a fraction of the samples. The method scales efficiently, completing fine-tuning on a GPU within a quarter of an hour for a batch of one hundred samples (approximately 15 minutes for ten times more data), cutting costs and time drastically when handling much larger unlabelled datasets as well.

Formal verification techniques have historically focused on ensuring the correctness of components within software systems, leaving methods for assessing entire systems under broad operational ranges notably absent. This paper introduces a formal framework dedicated to program evaluation, designed to address such program-wide questions. We propose evaluating a program by analyzing a state-transition diagram known as its computation tree. Using tree invariants allows us to answer key query types, including whether a program remains safe against specified violations, and by examining path invariants and control trees—both condensed representations of the computation tree—we address questions regarding reachability and liveness. A central distinction of our approach lies in how it condenses the computation tree into various invariant forms to facilitate such assessments. We demonstrate the framework's practical application by formally resolving specific queries related to the well-known ByPass security vulnerability and verifying several temporal properties of Java's concurrent HashMap data structure.

Accurately determining a network's scale is critical for effective size-based resource allocation and limit setting. This study addresses the challenge of estimating the size of small-world graphs when confronted with multiple Byzantine failures, a group where adversaries can act based on knowledge of the algorithm and coordinate their actions, yet appear legitimate to others. The proposed algorithm operates in rounds, where an explorer node utilizes local information to navigate the graph, count distinct visited nodes, and infer the total population. We formalize complexity through two primary exploration phases and establish that the proposed method requires $O(\frac{n^{0.55}f^{0.95}}{\epsilon^2})$ round communications to estimate the size of a graph containing $n$ nodes with precision $\epsilon$, despite the presence of up to $f$ Byzantine nodes. Additionally, we establish a lower bound on communication overhead of $\Omega(n^{0.5})$, confirming the efficiency of our approach relative to theoretical limits. To validate these findings, we implemented extensive simulations comparing our estimator against prior methods developed for node-counting in power-law and ring topologies without consideration of faults.

Open-domain commonsense question answering (OPQA) represents a significant and engaging challenge within the NLP community. SEEM is introduced to address this through a process-oriented methodology that mirrors human reflective question-solving strategies. This framework includes synthesizing broad insights via a Rejection Sampling-based Reordering (RSR) operator and transforming these insights into precise responses through a Coarse-to-Precise Conversion (EVC) mechanism. Testing on two distinct open-domain datasets demonstrates significant improvements in answer accuracy compared to direct generation methods and existing answer enhancement techniques. These results highlight the effectiveness of SEEM in bridging coarse generative capabilities with precise response formation in open-domain QA systems.

Spectral models of the molecular cations abundant in comet environments are frequently constructed using data from terrestrial experiments, despite the inherent uniqueness of this class of resonating-valence-bond (RVB) oxygen-based radicals. A detailed analysis of available UV absorption measurements for seven such cations exposes significant gaps regarding bond lengths, equilibrium energies, and harmonic vibration frequencies. These deficiencies stem largely from challenges in obtaining high-quality data in the vacuum ultraviolet range. Furthermore, a direct comparison between empirical results and theoretical predictions indicates substantial discrepancies in calculated long-range potential curves based on configuration interaction theories, as well as those utilizing semi-empirical methods alone, when applied directly to spectral fitting. Consequently, we propose refined theoretical approaches: adjusting calculated long-range potentials to match experimental short-range data and integrating measured spectra into the analysis of five of these cations to derive space-conditioned structural parameters. Finally, we present updated structural estimates and associated uncertainty ranges for all studied ions, recommending these refined values for utilization in modeling the neutral UV emission spectra of comets.

We address a critical challenge in machine learning: how to acquire model capabilities for tasks outside the current dataset's scope. We focus on this by asking can we use stochasticity to learn from varied datasets? We call our technique Random Stroll. The basic concept involves sharing data samples randomly among participants, allowing each party to train a local copy of the model and redistribute it, so that no raw samples leave their local storage. The process begins with at least one contributor providing training data containing the ability to perform on a broader range of inputs, ensuring that every participant can eventually access a model trained on heterogeneous sources. We show the effectiveness of Random Stroll by testing it in a real-world scenario where students in a classroom setting shared their notes to improve an automatic grading system for questions that did not have reference answers available.

The genesis, evolution, and demise of Population III (the primordial) stars remain an unverified but pivotal aspect of cosmic history. Pop III stars are known to be extremely massive; consequently, their remnants must form an over-massive X-ray binary (OXRB), defined here by a neutron star and black hole where both components exceed 30 and 80 solar masses respectively—combinations that typically produce OXRBs capable of generating observable gravitational radiation. We analyze OXRB dynamics within dense clusters surrounding supermassive black holes in galaxies and narrow down the feasible parameter space for these primordial systems. Such overdense clusters containing numerous neutron stars and black holes can also host gravitational radiation from mergers, offering a plausible pathway for early detection via current or upcoming observatories. Finding an OXRB originating from Population III stars would provide definitive evidence confirming both the existence and development of these initial stars.
